overview: The atlas’s “Tungus” is not the name of one state ruling this enormous Transbaikal-to-Amur polygon. “Tungus” became widespread through Russian records centuries later, while modern “Tungusic” names a language family whose early geography remains debated. For 700 to 1000, written neighbors mention Mohe groupings and, late in the interval, Jurchen. Archaeologists distinguish local Naifeld, Troitsky, and other material traditions, but pots, genes, speech, and political allegiance do not map automatically onto one another. Evidence is richest near the Amur, Zeya, Shilka, Sungari, and Primorye, not across every forest the map colors. Some households farmed millet or other crops, kept pigs or horses, fished, hunted, gathered plants, and moved seasonally; the mixture varied sharply. Semi-subterranean homes, handmade pottery, fortified places, bronze recycling, and burial grounds reveal skilled communities linked to Balhae, Tang, Turkic, and later Khitan worlds without proving a single “Tungus civilization.” The exact id vanishes at 1000, leaving many probes blank and later labels only partly overlapping it. That seam marks an atlas choice, not extinction, conquest of everyone, or the end of Tungusic-speaking communities.

periods.title: 700 to 713: a map umbrella beside a new Balhae state
periods.summary: Balhae had been founded in 698 to the south and southeast of much of the atlas polygon. Communities called Mohe in Chinese records occupied several regions and did not suddenly merge into one northern government in 700. The atlas opening is therefore a teaching boundary, not a coronation.

periods.title: 713 to 725: recognition, diplomacy, and different northern communities
periods.summary: Tang recognition helped formalize Balhae’s place in regional diplomacy after 713. Farther north, multiple Mohe groupings maintained their own relationships and movements. A court title sent to one ruler cannot be painted across every Amur, Shilka, and forest community included by this much larger atlas feature.

periods.title: 725 to 762: Blackwater offices existed mostly on paper and through envoys
periods.summary: Chinese records describe Tang titles and offices for Blackwater Mohe leaders during the eighth century. Such arrangements document diplomacy, tribute, and attempts to organize a frontier from the court’s viewpoint. They do not demonstrate routine Tang administration inside every settlement or direct obedience by all northern households.

periods.title: 762 to 800: overlapping ties resist a simple empire map
periods.summary: Heishui communities could deal with Balhae, Tang, and steppe powers in overlapping ways. Scholarship cautions against narrating those ties as a neat march from independence to subordination. Mobility, local rivalries, marriage, trade, and tribute could connect the same leaders to several political worlds at once.

periods.title: 800 to 840: regional traditions stay visible in ordinary objects
periods.summary: Naifeld and Troitsky archaeological groups remained distinguishable through pottery, settlement, and mortuary evidence. Those patterns help organize finds, but they are scholarly categories rather than passports. The eighth and ninth centuries show regional interaction and movement without reducing every maker of a certain pot to one named people.

periods.title: 840 to 900: a workshop turns imported styles into local objects
periods.summary: At late ninth-century Osinovoye Ozero, a craft worker melted bronze in a crucible supported inside a vessel-like furnace. Some Turkic-style plaques had been recast repeatedly and were likely raw material for Mohe ornaments. The workshop makes exchange tangible without turning style into ethnicity.

periods.title: 900 to 926: Jurchen enters records while older labels continue
periods.summary: A scholarly review places the first documented appearance of the Jurchen name in 903. That new outsider label did not instantly replace Mohe, identify every Tungusic speaker, or create a unified Jurchen state. Naming practices shifted as Khitan power rose and Balhae remained a major neighbor until 926.

periods.title: 926 to 960: Balhae falls, but northern communities do not vanish
periods.summary: Khitan forces defeated Balhae in 926. Refugees, local settlements, crafts, and political ties continued under changed conditions, and the atlas still keeps its broad Tungus color. Balhae’s fall matters regionally, but it cannot serve as a single ending for every community inside the target polygon.

periods.title: 960 to 1000: settlements continue across the atlas endpoint
periods.summary: A Shilka fortified settlement dated around the turn of the first and second millennia preserves about thirty large semi-subterranean house depressions and an ordered plan. Its excavators connect it with westward Mohe movement, an interpretation that demonstrates continuity and mobility rather than an exact 1000 collapse.

sections.title: What the map labels, and what it cannot prove

items.text: The index has one exact tungus-700 record, marked as a circa culture from 700 to 1000, and it lacks a card. Separate records called tungus and tungusic-tribes cover different centuries. Reusing either card would erase chronology and attach later evidence to the wrong feature.

The exact id occurs only in world-700, world-800, and world-900. Each file contains one polygon with one ring, but the coordinate sequence changes each time. The shape is an editorial regional envelope, not a surveyed boundary, treaty line, or proof of a centralized polity.

All three shapes stretch from Transbaikal across the Amur basin toward the lower Amur, with fixed probes near Chita, Nerchinsk, Zeya, Khabarovsk, and Nikolaevsk inside. That sweep joins very different ecologies and communities. One color cannot establish one economy, language, or self-name.

At 700 the target shares border arcs with Göktürk and Paleo-Siberian labels. At 800 it meets Uyghur and Paleo-Siberian labels; at 900 Liao and Oghuz labels also appear. Those are topology neighbors in this atlas, not evidence that every neighboring household recognized a crisp international frontier.

The exact shape is absent by world-1000 and remains absent in 1100, while many fixed probes become unlabeled. A smaller tungusic-tribes feature appears only in 1200, and a later siberians label covers other space by 1279. Neither is a safe successor to this card.

“Tungus” is a retrospective label here. A Russian Academy linguistic study finds that the ethnonym spread widely in Russian historical sources only from the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, long after this card. It should not be presented as an eighth-century common self-name across the polygon.

Modern “Tungusic” refers to a family of related languages, not a medieval passport. Proposed Proto-Tungusic homelands include Baikal, the middle Amur, Lake Khanka, and the Yalu region. Debate itself is evidence against drawing one certain origin point from the atlas’s very broad shape.

Chinese sources used Mohe for several named groupings, including Sumo and Heishui. Their reported locations, alliances, and power differed. “Mohe” therefore offers closer period vocabulary than “Tungus,” but it still cannot be substituted for every person, language, or archaeological assemblage inside the target.

Archaeologists distinguish Naifeld, Troitsky, and other Mohe culture groups through pottery, settlements, and burials. Correlating those material groups with the named peoples in texts remains interpretive. A pot can reveal a manufacturing tradition; it cannot introduce its maker by language, ancestry, and political loyalty.

The Jurchen name appears in surviving written records near the end of this card, with one study dating its first documented use to 903. That is a change in recorded terminology, not proof that everyone previously called Mohe adopted one new identity on a single morning.

sections.title: Rivers, fields, forests, and varied food

items.text: Historical descriptions associate some Mohe communities with plough cultivation, millet, wheat, soybeans, mallow, horses, pigs, dogs, and hunting. Those lists come through outsider texts and cover particular groups. They should widen the menu, not become one compulsory shopping list for every northern household.

Archaeology in Primorye finds farming, animal keeping, hunting, fishing, gathering, and use of marine and river resources in the sixth to early eighth centuries. Researchers could not securely rank their importance. That honest uncertainty is more useful than assigning every family an identical economic pie chart.

At one coastal site, shells and remains from eight marine fish species show detailed use of local waters. Elsewhere, river fish or terrestrial animals could matter more. Food evidence is wonderfully specific and stubbornly local, which is why a clam shell should not govern supper across the entire Amur basin.

Stable carbon and nitrogen isotopes from people buried at Troitskiy indicate diets dominated by animal products with a smaller contribution from plants, mainly C3 plants. That result describes sampled individuals at one cemetery. It does not cancel textual and botanical evidence for farming elsewhere.

Seasonal movement toward rivers and pastures appears in Chinese descriptions of Mohe life, while fortified and unfortified settlements show that mobility and residence could coexist. Families might return to substantial homes and also use temporary places. “Mobile” and “settled” are not mutually exclusive boxes.

sections.title: Houses, hearths, forts, and settlement plans

items.text: Western Amur excavations distinguish several house forms: sunken frame-and-post buildings, ground-level structures, and lighter seasonal shelters. Hearths might sit centrally or near a wall, and construction details varied between archaeological groups. There was no single regulation hut issued to everyone labeled Tungus by the atlas.

Troitsky-group houses at sites such as Osinovoye Ozero could have deep rectangular or square floor pits, roof supports, recessed entrances, and storage niches. These features reveal planning and repeated household labor. They do not tell us every resident’s name, language, or relationship to the others.

Early medieval fortresses included promontory sites using steep terrain and valley sites on floodplains, with earthen or stone ramparts and protected gates. Fortification shows organized work and concern about danger. It does not prove a single empire built every wall or commanded all surrounding settlements.

Near the Shilka, a turn-of-millennium settlement has roughly thirty large semi-subterranean dwelling depressions arranged in lines, perhaps around a shared central space. The plan hints at collective decisions and neighborhood order, while excavation is still needed before assigning exact functions to every empty patch.

The 900 geometry withdraws slightly northward along its southern edge while fixed central probes remain inside. That cartographic change cannot be matched automatically to a migration, war, or fort-building episode. Archaeological site chronologies and map polygons were made from different evidence and at different scales.

sections.title: Pottery, metal, exchange, and practical achievement

items.text: A late ninth-century craft worker at Osinovoye Ozero used a crucible on a ceramic support inside a vessel-like furnace. Excavators reconstructed casting molds and finishing methods from tools and debris. The evidence captures skilled hands at work, not an anonymous people waiting for outsiders to bring technology.

Nine bronze plaques from the workshop fell into different compositional groups, and some had been remelted repeatedly. Turkic-style pieces were probably recycled into locally characteristic ornaments. Metal crossed cultural lines, then became something new; fashion traveled, but it did not carry an ethnicity certificate.

Eighth to tenth century Amur finds include bronze, silver, and gold ornaments as well as a Kaiyuan Tongbao coin at Osinovoye Ozero. Material analysis reveals metal choices and recycling. A coin can demonstrate contact or circulation, but it cannot by itself prove taxes, citizenship, or direct Tang rule.

Handmade pots, wheel-finished vessels, jars, and vases varied by archaeological group. Troitsky cemetery alone yielded more than fifty intact handmade vessels and thousands of fragments. Pottery records choices in clay, forming, firing, use, and burial, making ordinary containers one of archaeology’s busiest witnesses.

Tang court records list tribute and regional products, but tribute was diplomacy as well as exchange. Sable pelts, animal products, horses, titles, and gifts moved through selective encounters. These lists foreground what courts wanted to record, not every object traded between neighboring families or carried along rivers.

sections.title: Families, children, social life, and learning

items.text: No exact-period source consulted supplies a universal family diagram. Houses, cemeteries, food remains, tools, and settlement plans show people living and working in groups, but kinship labels rarely survive. Archaeologists can identify repeated household activity without deciding that every hearth belonged to one nuclear family.

Children certainly learned language, routes, plants, animals, craft steps, and social expectations, yet the evidence does not document a common school system across this region. Learning probably happened through observation, practice, correction, and stories. “Probably” matters here because no excavated lesson plan was tucked under a pot.

Burial grounds show long-lived communities attending to the dead. At Troitskiy, excavated rites include primary burial, secondary burial, and cremation in unequal proportions. Those choices required memory and cooperation, but they do not allow us to reconstruct every household’s beliefs or grief.

Amur museum collections include vessels, belt fittings, earrings, bells, beads, weapons, and symbolic objects from burial settings. Grave goods reveal what mourners selected for a particular rite, not a complete household inventory. The fanciest belt buckle was not necessarily daily playground equipment.

Historical accounts describe clothing, braided hair, woven materials, and regional head ornaments, while archaeology preserves only some fibers and fittings. Dress could signal age, status, place, or occasion. One vivid description should be treated as a local glimpse, not a mandatory costume for millions of square kilometers.

sections.title: Health, healing, bodies, and evidence gaps

items.text: The isotope study offers evidence about food intake, not a full medical chart. Diets rich in animal protein may reflect available foods, status, season, or local practice, but isotope ratios do not diagnose a person’s favorite meal, illness, or treatment. Health claims need different evidence.

One osteological study examined only ten Troitskiy crania, five classified male and five female. Such a small cemetery sample cannot define the bodies of every Mohe group, much less everyone beneath the atlas label. Measurements are observations; sweeping racial or linguistic conclusions would outrun them.

Seven wild plant species found in a nearby early medieval economic study may have served as food and perhaps medicine. “Perhaps” must stay attached. A seed can show presence and sometimes processing, but it cannot name a recipe, dosage, healer, or diagnosis without stronger contextual evidence.

Burial evidence can reveal healed injuries, stress, age, or diet when preservation and analysis allow, yet funerary treatment is not medical treatment. Secondary burial and cremation describe what communities did after death. They should not be repackaged as evidence for how fever, childbirth, or wounds were managed.

No consulted exact-period source securely describes physicians, midwives, named remedies, or a shared healing institution across the target. That absence is an archive limit, not proof that people lacked care. Families still nursed, warmed, fed, splinted, soothed, and experimented, but the details remain undocumented.

sections.title: Water, waste, sanitation, and the toilet question

items.text: Settlements clustered along the Amur and its tributaries, and several fixed atlas probes follow those river corridors. Rivers supported travel, fishing, and access to water, but proximity alone does not prove how drinking water was collected, stored, boiled, or protected in any particular house.

Semi-subterranean houses contained hearths, entrances, roof supports, floors, and sometimes storage niches. Published descriptions consulted for this card do not identify a standard indoor toilet. A floor pit needs contextual analysis before anyone promotes it to a latrine; archaeology dislikes ambitious plumbing guesses.

Valley fortresses occupied floodplains and used earth, stone, ramparts, and gates. Their builders had to manage wet ground and runoff, but a defensive ditch is not automatically a drain or sewer. Similar-looking cuts can serve very different jobs, and contents, slope, and connections matter.

Food processing, animals, fires, pottery, and crowded homes necessarily produced ash, bones, broken objects, dung, and other waste. Archaeologists can study deposits, yet the reviewed publications do not establish one regional sanitation rule. Practice likely varied by settlement, season, house, and available space.

Toilet verdict: no securely identified exact-period toilet can be assigned to every community under this atlas label. People obviously relieved themselves, but location and cleanup are not documented uniformly. The honest card leaves the royal flush out, along with the lazy claim that missing pipes meant missing hygiene.

sections.title: Writing, outsider voices, and one careful sample

items.text: No securely localized Tungusic-language sentence from 700 to 1000 survives in the consulted evidence. Jurchen texts belong to the later Jin period and remain only partly deciphered; Manchu is much later. Reconstructed Proto-Tungusic words are scholarly reconstructions, not quotations from a medieval speaker.

A contemporaneous outsider sample is “黑水靺鞨,” transliterated Hēishuǐ Mòhé and translated “Blackwater Mohe.” It appears as a group name in the Tang Huiyao, a Chinese institutional history completed in 961. The genre is court historiography, not a Tungusic sentence, autograph, or self-name.

The same Chinese compilation describes offices, tribute, leaders, and group divisions through an imperial administrative lens. It preserves precious evidence and a viewpoint with political goals. Its neat categories should be compared with archaeology, not copied directly onto every household inside the much larger atlas polygon.

The label “Jurchen” entering records in 903 is also outsider documentation. Later spellings and classifications changed across Liao, Goryeo, and other sources. A recorded name tells us how a writer categorized people in a situation; it may not preserve their pronunciation or preferred identity.

Likewise, “Tungus” belongs to a much later documentary history. Its debated etymology and Russian-era spread make it unsuitable as the sample word for this card. Showing a later label in old-looking type would be visually charming and historically upside down, so the card refuses the trick.

Tang titles for Blackwater leaders show diplomatic contact and claims of authority, but distance and local autonomy limited what a court appointment could do. An office recorded in a capital archive does not prove tax collectors, judges, or soldiers appeared routinely in every Amur settlement.

Balhae was a powerful state with capitals, provinces, art, Buddhism, and wide diplomatic exchange. Some Mohe communities were within or connected to it, while others remained outside, resisted, or negotiated separately. Balhae should appear as a neighbor and participant, not swallow the whole Tungus polygon.

Heishui relations with Balhae, Tang, and Turkic powers could overlap rather than follow a single ladder of submission. Leaders might exchange tribute, titles, goods, or military support in different directions. Frontier politics resembled a web of choices more than one row of colored blocks.

Khitan conquest ended Balhae in 926, changing regional power and movement. It did not erase northern settlements or make all later Jurchen communities identical descendants of one state. The Shilka settlement near 1000 is one material reminder that people reorganized and continued.

At world-1000 the exact id disappears without one replacement covering the same probes. The safest ending is continuity: families still built, cooked, traveled, learned, traded, buried relatives, fetched water, and argued about chores. The software stops saying Tungus; people do not stop existing.

ending.text: The exact tungus-700 id ends at 1000 because the atlas removes its broad regional label. Many fixed probes become blank, and no single successor covers the same geometry. Balhae had fallen to Khitan forces in 926, while Mohe and emerging Jurchen names, settlements, craft traditions, languages, and families continued through changing political networks. The later tungusic-tribes and siberians records are chronologically and geometrically different, so this card does not inherit them or claim a clean ethnic handoff. The endpoint is an editorial seam, not the extinction, conquest, or disappearance of every community represented imperfectly by the atlas umbrella.
